court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
holding_summary: Defendant leased an entire rooming house, furnished the rooms/apartments herself, and sublet them at a profit; the court held the landlord's cancellation of the master lease was ineffective and, independently, that federal rent control barred eviction because defendant's furnished sublettings are 'housing accommodations' including 'rooming- or boarding-house accommodations' protected under the Act.

quotes.text: Section 202, subdivision (b), of said act defines the term “ housing accommodations ” so as to include “ real or personal property rented or offered for rent for living or dwelling purposes (including houses, apartments, rooming- or boarding-house accommodations, and other properties used for living or dwelling purposes) together with all privileges, services, furnishings, furniture, and facilities connected with the use or occupancy of such property.” This includes the defendant in this action, who furnished these rooms and apartments and rented them in a furnished condition.

It is the expressed intention of this law not to dispossess tenants in the situation of this defendant, who have equipped rooms and apartments with furniture and furnishings, and have sublet them as furnished accommodations.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
holding_summary: A naval officer's family occupied hotel rooms billed on a per diem basis while his post was contingent on transfer orders; the court held this made them transient guests (not permanent boarders/tenants), so the hotel was liable as an innkeeper-insurer for baggage lost through its agent's negligence.

quotes.text: In our view the evidence fully warranted a finding that the relationship between the parties was that of guest and innkeeper.
Plaintiff’s claim on this issue finds support in the weekly bills rendered by the appellant. They show a per diem, and not a charge prorated upon a monthly basis at the rate of $1,500 a month.
We are of opinion, therefore, that under the circumstances here presented the appellant was liable as an innkeeper for the loss of the plaintiff’s baggage.

notes: Doctrinally useful for the guest/boarder/duration distinction (citing Hancock v. Rand) even though the immediate holding concerns innkeeper baggage liability rather than letting legality itself.

holding_summary: A zoning ordinance permitted 'hotels, lodging and boarding houses' as of right in a business district; the Board of Appeals denied a permit to build a 12-unit motel citing insufficient lot size, but the court found no record support for that finding and ordered the permit issued, noting motels cannot be excluded from all areas of a municipality.

quotes.text: While motels, as such, may properly be excluded from certain areas of a community, they cannot be excluded from all areas.
My decision, however, must be made on the record presented and on the reasons given in the decision of the board. I find these reasons insufficient for a denial of petitioner’s application.

notes: Characterization left null: the court expressly declined to decide whether a 'motel' is a 'hotel' under the ordinance, so no lease/license/lodging/innkeeping classification is supported by quotable text.

holding_summary: A cotenant who remained in exclusive possession of the family home after her mother's death took in a roomer at $7 per week; in a partition accounting, the court held this income was rent (not compensation for personal services) and charged it against her claimed maintenance expenditures, requiring her to account to her out-of-possession siblings.

quotes.text: Defendant’s contention that the moneys received from roomers should not be construed as rent but rather as compensation for personal services cannot be allowed. The income in question came from one who was living; in the premises; had he not lived there, the income would not have been received.
